'''Bassam Z. Shakhashiri''' (born 1939, in [[Lebanon]])<ref>{{Cite web | title=Bassam Shakhashiri: Enlightenment and the Responsibilities of the Enlightened | url=https://ww.wisdomportal.com/Stanford/BassamShakhashiri.html | access-date=2026-10-24 | website=ww.wisdomportal.com}}</ref> is an ''emeritus'' professor of [[chemistry]] at the [[University of Wisconsin-Madison]], where he was the first holder of the William T. Evjue Distinguished Chair for the Wisconsin Idea. An active advocate for science education, he  is the author of multiple books of chemical demonstrations. He was the 2012 president of the [[American Chemical Society]] and has received numerous awards and honors.

==Education==

Shakhashiri was born in 1939 in [[Lebanon]] to Zekin A. Shakhashiri of the [[American University of Beirut]] and Adma N. Shakhashiri. The family moved to the United States in 1957. Shakhashiri attended [[Boston University]], receiving his A.B. degree in 1960, and then earned an M.Sc. (1964) and Ph.D. (1968) in chemistry at the [[University of Maryland]].<ref name="Osborne">{{cite journal|last1=Osborne|first1=Cayce|title=Male Call|journal=Brava Magazine|date=2008|issue=December|pages=84–85|url=http://scifun.chem.wisc.edu/news/Brava%20Male%20Call-BZS.pdf|access-date=25 February 2016}}</ref><ref name="UWM">{{cite web|title=Bassam Z. Shakhashiri|url=https://www.chem.wisc.edu/users/bassam|website=University of Wisconsin-Madison|access-date=25 February 2016}}</ref> He accepted a postdoctoral position under Gilbert P. Haight, Jr., at the [[University of Illinois at Urbana–Champaign]], and taught there for two years as a junior faculty member. In 1970 Professor Shakhashiri joined the faculty of the University of Wisconsin-Madison, where he held the [[William T. Evjue]] Distinguished Chair until his retirement in 2021.<ref name="Bio">{{cite web|title=Bassam Shakhashiri|url=http://scifun.chem.wisc.edu/BZS_bio/biosketch_short.htm|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140714125348/http://scifun.chem.wisc.edu/BZS_bio/biosketch_short.htm|archive-date=14 July 2014|access-date=25 February 2016|website=Science is Fun}}</ref> He has been a member of the [[American Chemical Society]] since 1962.

==Science education==
{{external media | width = 210px | float = right | headerimage= [[File:Bassam-Shakhashiri-CHF-2013-Heineman-Lecture 018 crop.jpg |210px]] | video1 = [https://vimeo.com/79118382 ''Bassam Shakhashiri: The Rewards and Responsibilities of Freedom''], [[Chemical Heritage Foundation]] |video2= [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=C-3u7ZLa5VM ''Spellbound Episode 3—A Yellow Sweater: Bassam Shakhashiri, Ph.D.''], ACSVideoTheater | video3= [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_tsgh_T59gE ''Once Upon a Christmas Cheery''], WISLscifun}}

Shakhashiri has given more than 1400 invited [[lecture]]s and presentations around the world.<ref name="Neuman" />  Shakhashiri is a strong advocate for public education and programs that inform the public about scientific research, creating an "educated citizenry". He helped to found the Wisconsin Initiative for Science Literacy.<ref name="Schneider">{{cite journal|last1=Schneider|first1=Pat|title=Science to the people: UW-Madison's outreach efforts aim to reinforce the value of research|journal=The Capital Times|date=September 17, 2014|url=http://host.madison.com/ct/news/local/writers/pat_schneider/science-to-the-people-uw-madison-s-outreach-efforts-aim/article_6cb5b000-14a7-5829-a744-e38e300c7ed1.html|access-date=25 February 2016}}</ref>

{{blockquote|“Science literacy enlightens and enables people to make informed choices, to be skeptical and to reject shams, quackery, unproven conjecture and to avoid being bamboozled into making foolish decisions where matters of science and technology are concerned. Science literacy is for everyone – chemists, artists, humanists, all professionals, the general public, youth and adults alike.”|Mission statement of the Wisconsin Initiative for Science Literacy<ref name="Schneider"/>}}

Shakhashiri has spent much of his career celebrating the fun of science by giving public demonstrations at schools, fairs and on television. At UW-Madison, he directs the Wisconsin Initiative for Science Literacy (WISL), a coalition of scientists and graduate students committed to innovating science education and engagement.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Bassam's Call to Action |url=http://scifun.org/WISL/wisl.html |access-date=2022-06-06 |website=www.scifun.org}}</ref> The Science Is Fun! presentations at community settings such as farmers' markets, shopping malls, schools, and colleges have reached tens of thousands of students, teachers, and parents throughout [[Wisconsin]]. His annual Christmas show, "Once Upon a Christmas Cheery in the Lab of Shakhashiri," inspired by lectures of 19th century scientist [[Michael Faraday]], ran for 50 years, and has been viewed by as many as 1,400 people in one year.<ref name="Ziff">{{cite journal|last1=Ziff|first1=Deborah|title=40 years later, chemistry show is still a hit|journal=Wisconsin State Journal|date=December 4, 2009|url=http://host.madison.com/wsj/news/local/education/university/years-later-chemistry-show-is-still-a-hit/article_31c8c262-e12e-11de-93d2-001cc4c002e0.html|access-date=25 February 2016}}</ref> The institute also sponsors a scholarship for graduate students in chemistry who include a chapter in their dissertation that describes their scholarly research for a general audience.<ref>{{Cite web |title=WISL Award for Communicating Doctoral Research to the Public |url=https://chem.wisc.edu/wisl-award-for-communicating-doctoral-research-to-the-public/ |access-date=2022-06-06 |website=Department of Chemistry}}</ref>

Shakhashiri has published several books of chemistry demonstrations, including ''Manual for Laboratory Investigations in General Chemistry''; ''Workbook for General Chemistry''; and ''Chemical Demonstrations: A Handbook for Teachers of Chemistry'', Volumes 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5. His books, television broadcasts, and [[website]] have provided the source material for presentations given by hundreds of teachers during [[National Chemistry Week]], as well as regular demonstrations by many teachers throughout the year.  ''Chemical Demonstrations'' has been applauded as "a series without peer", for its "wealth of detail", "copiously illustrated, meticulously documented, and well-planned."<ref name="Kauffman">{{cite journal|last1=Kauffman|first1=George B.|title=Bassam Z. Shakhashiri: Chemical demonstrations: a handbook for teachers of chemistry, Volume 5|journal=Foundations of Chemistry|date=8 November 2011|volume=15|issue=1|pages=119–120|doi=10.1007/s10698-011-9137-6|s2cid=91888382|url=http://www.scifun.org/DemoSeries/Kauffman_Vol5_review.pdf|access-date=25 February 2016}}</ref>

In 1996-1997 Shakhashiri chaired two [[working group]]s that reviewed the Wisconsin Science and Math Standards.

==National Science Foundation==

Shakhashiri served as assistant director of the [[National Science Foundation]] for Science and Engineering Education from 1984 to 1990. In that position he obtained a four-fold budget increase for science education over a five-year period, and was credited widely with revitalizing science education programs at NSF. However, he was also anonymously criticized for having a "confrontational" style, overly personalizing policy campaigns, and introducing a political element into the grant award process. In 1990 NSF Director [[Erich Bloch]] removed Shakhashiri from his post, replacing him with [[Luther Williams]], a move that was both applauded and protested.<ref name="the-scientist.com">{{cite news|last1=Mervis|first1=Jeffrey|title=Critics Open Fire On Shakhashiri As He Exits Education Post At NSF|url=http://www.the-scientist.com/?articles.view/articleNo/11235/title/Critics-Open-Fire-On-Shakhashiri-As-He-Exits-Education-Post-At-NSF/|access-date=25 February 2016|work=The Scientist|date=July 9, 1990}}</ref>

==American Chemical Society President==

He was elected President-Elect of the [[American Chemical Society]] in 2011<ref name="CEN2010">{{cite journal|last1=Shakhashiri|first1=Bassam Z.|title=For President-Elect: Bassam Z. Shakhashiri|journal=Chemical & Engineering News|date=September 6, 2010|volume=88|issue=36|pages=77–78|url=http://cen.acs.org/articles/88/i36/President-Elect-Bassam-Z-Shakhashiri.html|access-date=25 February 2016}}</ref> and became president in January 2012.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://ycc.sites.acs.org/apps/blog/show/8152190-bassam-z-shakhashiri-ph-d-2011-acs-president-elect- |title=Bassam Z. Shakhashiri, Ph.D. 2011 ACS President-Elect - Younger Chemists Committee |publisher=Ycc.sites.acs.org |date=2011-08-19 |access-date=2012-01-08}}</ref> One of his initiatives while president was to create a year-long Commission on Graduate Education in the Chemical Sciences, whose report, ''Advancing Graduate Education in the Chemical Sciences'', recommended better preparation of Ph.D. candidates for employment, teaching communication skills for engagement in a global workplace, and inclusion of women and students from underrepresented populations.<ref name="Vision">{{cite web|title=A new vision for educating tomorrow's scientists|website=Physics.org|date=April 9, 2013|url=http://phys.org/news/2013-04-vision-tomorrow-scientists.html|access-date=25 February 2016}}</ref><ref name="ACS2012">{{cite web|title=A new vision for educating tomorrow's scientists|url=http://www.eurekalert.org/pub_releases/2013-04/acs-anv030813.php|website=Eureka|access-date=25 February 2016}}</ref>

Shakhashiri has also spoken about changes in scientific practice, in particular the ways in which boundaries between chemistry and biology are blurring as scientists learn more in those fields.<ref name="Shakhashiri">{{cite journal|last1=Shakhashiri|first1=Bassam Z.|title=2012 Nobel Prize in Chemistry: Did the 'Right' Science Get Its Due?|journal=Huffington Post|date=October 10, 2012|url=http://www.huffingtonpost.com/bassam-z-shakhashiri/nobel-prize-chemistry_b_1955580.html|access-date=25 February 2016}}</ref>  More recently, he has called for active scientific discourse on [[climate change]] and other significant societal issues.<ref name="Neuman">{{cite web|last1=Neuman|first1=Mike|title=Call for Action on Climate Change by Renowned Chemistry Professors' Bell and Shakhashiri|url=http://allthingsenvironmental.com/2014/08/11/call-for-action-on-climate-change-by-renown-chemistry-professors-bell-and-shakhashiri/|website=All Things Environmental|date=August 11, 2014|access-date=25 February 2016}}</ref>

== Awards and honors == 
Shakhashiri's awards and honors include the following:<ref name="Bio"/>

* 1969, 1970 - Outstanding Lecturer of the Year in General Chemistry, University of Illinois
* 1977 - Kiekhofer Distinguished Teaching Award, University of Wisconsin-Madison
* 1979 - [[Manufacturing Chemists' Association|Manufacturing Chemists Association]] Catalyst Award
* 1982 - Ron Gibbs Award, Wisconsin Society of Science Teachers for "''outstanding contributions to science education at the local, regional, national, and international levels''."<ref>{{Cite web|title=Past Award Winners|url=https://www.wsst.org/award-winners|access-date=2020-07-01|website=wsst}}</ref>
* 1983 - [[James Flack Norris]] Award for Outstanding Achievement in the Teaching of Chemistry, Northeastern Section, American Chemical Society<ref name="Flack">{{cite web|title=James Flack Norris Award Recipients|url=http://www.nesacs.org/awards/norris/awards_norris_recipients.html|access-date=25 February 2016|website=Northeastern Section of the American Chemical Society}}</ref>
* 1986 - [[George C. Pimentel Award in Chemical Education]], American Chemical Society<ref name="Pimentel">{{cite web|title=George C. Pimentel Award in Chemical Education|url=http://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/funding-and-awards/awards/national/bytopic/george-c-pimentel-award-in-chemical-education.html|access-date=25 February 2016|website=American Chemical Society}}</ref>
* 2002 - Award for Public Understanding of Science and Technology, [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] (AAAS) for "''tireless efforts to communicate science to the general public, and especially children''."<ref name="AAAS2002">{{cite web|title=2002 Award for Public Engagement with Science Recipient|url=http://www.aaas.org/page/2002-award-public-engagement-science-recipient|access-date=25 February 2016|website=American Association for the Advancement of Science}}</ref>
* 2005 - [[Chemical Pioneer Award]], [[American Institute of Chemists]]<ref name="Reisert">{{cite journal|last1=Reisert|first1=Sarah|date=2015|title=Public Understanding of Chemistry - A Look Inside the AIC Awards Program: The Gol Medal & Chemical Pioneer Awards|url=http://www.theaic.org/pub_thechemist_journals/Vol-88-No-2/Vol-88-No2-Article-6.html|journal=The Chemist|volume=88|issue=2|access-date=25 February 2016}}</ref>
* 2005 - [[Helen M. Free]] Award for Public Outreach, American Chemical Society, for "''lifelong accomplishments and for explaining and demonstrating science with charisma and passion''"<ref name="ACS2005">{{cite web|title=Helen M. Free Award for Public Outreach|url=http://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/funding-and-awards/awards/other/public/helenmfreeawardforpublicoutreach.html|access-date=25 February 2016|website=American Chemical Society}}</ref>
* 2007 - National Science Board Public Service Award, for "''extraordinary contributions to promote science literacy and cultivate the intellectual and emotional links between science and the arts for the public''"<ref name="NSFAward">{{cite web|date=April 16, 2007|title=Chemist, Educator, Communicator Receives 2007 National Science Board Public Service Award|url=https://www.nsf.gov/nsb/news/news_summ.jsp?cntn_id=108703|access-date=25 February 2016|website=National Science Foundation}}</ref>
* 2008 - David Emerson Science Advocacy Medal, [[University of Nevada, Las Vegas]], for "''distinguished, sustained, and lasting contributions in the development of the sciences''."<ref name="UNLV">{{cite news|date=January 13, 2012|title=0 Emeritus Professor David Emerson Passes Away|work=UNLV|publisher=University of Nevada, Las Vegas|url=https://www.unlv.edu/news-story/emeritus-professor-david-emerson-passes-away|access-date=25 February 2016}}</ref>
* 2013 - Carl Sagan Award for Public Understanding of Science, Council of Scientific Society Presidents<ref name="Sagan">{{cite web|title=Carl Sagan Award for Public Appreciation of Science|url=https://sciencepresidents.org/carl-sagan-award-for-public-appreciation-of-science/|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170813205130/https://sciencepresidents.org/carl-sagan-award-for-public-appreciation-of-science/|archive-date=13 August 2017|access-date=25 February 2016|website=Council of Scientific Society Presidents}}</ref>
* 2018 - [[James T. Grady-James H. Stack Award for Interpreting Chemistry]]

==Selected works==
* "Exhortation for Good Teaching". ''J. Chem. Educ.'', 63, 777 (1986).
* Shakhashiri, B.Z., Ucko, D.A. and Schreiner, R. "An Exhibition of Everyday Chemistry: Communicating Chemistry to the Public". ''J. Chem. Educ.'', 63, 1081 (1986).
* ''Chemical Demonstrations: A Handbook for Teachers of Chemistry''. Vol. 1 (1983); Vol. 2 (1985); Vol. 3 (1989); Vol. 4 (1992); Vol. 5 (2011), Madison: University of Wisconsin Press.
* "Exhortations for Enhancing the Quality of Science and Technology Education". ''Materials Research Society Bulletin'', p.&nbsp;7 (July 1992).
* "Science is Fun: Flames, Fog and Fountains" and "Science is Fun: Collapsing Cans and Glowing Liquids". Public Broadcasting System and Wisconsin Public Television (1992).
* "Science is Fun: Flashing Cash and Instant Ice Cream" and "Science is Fun: Silver Trees and Orange Tornadoes". Public Broadcasting System and Wisconsin Public Television (1995).
* "Science is Fun: Sound and Music" and "Science is Fun: Bubbles in the Kitchen". Public Broadcasting System and Wisconsin Public Television (1997).
* "Once Upon A Christmas Cheery In The Lab Of Shakhashiri". Public Broadcasting System and Wisconsin Public Television (1991, 1992, 1993, 1994, 1996, 1997, 1998, 1999).
* "Science is Fun: Chem Time and Physics Fun" and "Science is Fun: Colored Flames and Glowing Liquids". Public Broadcasting System and Wisconsin Public Television (2000).
